name: Epithalamin

lead: Epithalamin is a pineal-gland peptide extract developed in Russia by Khavinson's group, from which the tetrapeptide Epitalon was derived. Longevity enthusiasts use it hoping to slow ageing, including how old they look.

The chain runs from pineal peptides to melatonin and rhythm effects to slower visible ageing. The developing group reports longer lifespan in flies, mice and rats, and raised melatonin production in old rats. No randomized human trial was found.

paras: It is used in periodic courses within longevity routines, often discussed alongside Epitalon. Users generally describe long-horizon, general aims rather than quick visible results.
Human safety data was not found in the sources reviewed. It is an animal-derived preparation not approved in most countries.

angle.text: Epithalamin, the pineal extract behind Epitalon, is used by longevity enthusiasts hoping to slow ageing, including how old someone looks. Lifespan and melatonin effects are reported in animals; appearance has not been measured in people.

lead: Epithalamin is a peptide preparation extracted from the pineal gland of cattle, developed in Russia by the group of Vladimir Khavinson and, earlier, by Vladimir Dilman's laboratory, which isolated a biologically active pineal extract in 1979 and showed it stimulated melatonin production.[1] The synthetic tetrapeptide Epitalon (Ala-Glu-Asp-Gly) was later designed from its amino-acid composition.[2][3]

It has no established cosmetic use. It enters appearance discussions through the longevity and anti-aging end of the peptide world: people interested in slower ageing, better sleep rhythm through melatonin, and a more youthful look over the long term follow Epitalon and its parent extract. The chain is indirect and rests on the claim that supporting pineal function and antioxidant defences slows age-related decline.

Studies from the developing group report longer lifespan in fruit flies, mice and rats, raised melatonin output in old rats, and antioxidant effects.[4][5][6][7] The same group has also published small human studies, including randomized comparisons in elderly cardiac patients and a study of melatonin rhythm in healthy older people.[8][9] A 2026 narrative review notes that human evidence on the synthetic peptide is limited to small physiological or biomarker studies and that no adequately powered randomized trial has established therapeutic efficacy.[3]
infobox: Khavinson and Dilman groups, Russia (extract isolated 1979)

paras: A 2002 review by the developing group states that they built a technology for making complex peptide preparations from tissue extracts, including a pineal preparation, Epithalamin, which increased outgrowth of pineal explants in culture, increased melatonin production in rats, improved immune parameters in rats and mice, showed anticarcinogenic effects in experimental models and stimulated antioxidant defences.[10] The authors describe these effects as combining into the ability to extend lifespan in rats, mice and fruit flies.[10]

Epithalamin is a mixture of pineal polypeptides, not a single defined molecule. Epitalon is a synthetic tetrapeptide made from the amino-acid composition of Epithalamin, and a 2026 narrative review treats the two separately, describing Epithalamin as a chemically distinct pineal-derived polypeptide preparation and its studies as historical context.[2][3]

A 1994 review of artificial life extension recounts that Dilman and co-workers isolated a biologically active pineal extract from rats in 1979 and later showed that it stimulates melatonin production; it names this extract epithalamin.[1] The same account notes that Pierpaoli and co-workers gave melatonin directly to mice in 1987, and that both lines of work reported roughly a 25 percent lifespan increase with delayed senescence, and states that Dilman's group reported beneficial effects of epithalamin in humans.[1]

Later work by the Khavinson group published animal lifespan studies through the 1990s and reviewed twenty years of pineal peptide research in 1994.[11] In 2000 the group also reported the effect of the pineal tetrapeptide on antioxidant defence in Drosophila.[12] A 1979 Russian-language trial listing in the oncology literature concerns an epiphyseal polypeptide extract in cervical cancer, and a 1999 randomized study examined comprehensive treatment of poor-prognosis cervical cancer.[13][14]

The group proposes that Epithalamin acts through the pineal gland and its melatonin rhythm. In old rats it raised pineal and serum melatonin, and in the fruit-fly work it was compared head to head with melatonin for lifespan and free-radical oxidation.[5][4] Reviews from the group also describe antioxidant effects, including lowered peroxide chemiluminescence and changes in superoxide dismutase activity in aged rodent tissues, and restoration of age-related disturbance in pineal and pancreatic hormone function.[15][6][16]

A review of pineal and thymic peptides describes immunoendocrine interaction, in which pineal peptides such as Epithalamin and Epitalon showed a stronger protective effect on thymus involution than thymic peptides had on the pineal gland.[17] A separate 2003 oncology review discusses how pineal suppression, by pinealectomy or constant light, increases mammary carcinogenesis in rodents; this concerns the gland rather than Epithalamin specifically.[18]

A 1992 study reported an effect on lifespan and on pineal and serum melatonin in old rats.[5] A 1997 Drosophila study compared Epithalamin with melatonin for lifespan and free-radical oxidation.[4] A 1998 paper concluded from fruit-fly, mouse and rat data that Epithalamin increased lifespan.[6] A 1994 review covered twenty years of work in experimental gerontology and oncology.[11] Later papers reported restored hormonal function of the pineal gland and pancreas in age-related disturbance and antioxidant properties of pineal peptides.[16][7] Nearly all of these studies come from the group that developed the preparation.

Epithalamin is a regional, animal-derived preparation. Outside the former Soviet states it is far less visible than its synthetic descendant Epitalon, which circulates in research-peptide and longevity communities and is the subject of most recent reviews.[2][3] The 2026 review lists pharmacokinetic, dose-ranging, long-term safety, immunogenicity, product-quality and regulatory uncertainties for the synthetic peptide.[3]

Human studies exist but are small and come largely from the developing group. A randomized study in healthy elderly people examined the circadian rhythm of plasma melatonin before and after a course of Epithalamin: in people with initially low pineal activity melatonin rose in the dark period, while in those with normal function it tended to fall.[9]

In a randomized comparison reported in 2011, 39 coronary patients received courses of Epithalamin in addition to basic therapy for three years (six courses) while 40 controls received basic therapy alone; the authors reported slowed ageing of the cardiovascular system in the treated group, with 15-year follow-up.[8] The group has reported further randomized studies on blood pressure rhythm in women with ischaemic heart disease and hypertension, on survival in a pineal and thymic peptide study in older people, and on a pineal peptide complex and melatonin synthesis in elderly people.[19][20][21] The 2002 review by the group states that many animal effects were reproduced in clinical trials that, in its authors' words, demonstrated geroprotector activity in humans.[10]

The 2026 narrative review judges the human evidence for synthetic Epitalon to consist of small physiological or biomarker studies and an older controlled study in retinitis pigmentosa, and states that no adequately powered randomized trial has established therapeutic efficacy.[3] No study has measured skin, hair or facial appearance outcomes.
